lesson_title: A Pencil That Talks Across the Country
hook_text: A desk designed in Johannesburg, built in Port Elizabeth, and nobody made a single phone call. How?
clip_script: A designer in Johannesburg draws a school desk. A carpenter in Port Elizabeth, who has never met her, cuts every piece to size and joins it perfectly. No phone call, no email. The drawing did all the talking, because drawings have rules. Dark solid lines are edges you can see. Feint lines are the guide lines you drew first. Dashed lines are edges hidden behind something. A chain of long and short dashes marks a centre. Scale 1 to 2 means half size on paper, but the numbers always give the real size, in millimetres, with no mm written after them. That is the language. Free-hand sketching is the same language spoken fast: no ruler, loose grip, long strokes, feint first, dark after, labels on everything. Three quick sketches of your rescue device, each labelled, and you can show the whole class how it works without saying a word.
visual_style: Whiteboard desk drawing building up line type by line type, each type labelled as it appears, then a fast hand-sketch of a rescue device beside it.
mood: Quietly impressive, the rules revealed as a shared language.
pacing: Story hook, four line types in quick rhythm, scale and dimensions, then a burst of sketching.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sketch your rescue device three ways on squared paper.
